note: A dissent from the consensus: argues risk classification underweights circular effects, the difficulty of measuring risk at all, and geopolitical power imbalance.
title: Limitations of risk-based artificial intelligence regulation: a structuration theory approach
explain_beginner: Most countries now regulate AI by sorting systems into risk categories, with stricter rules for high-risk applications. This paper argues that approach has blind spots. It misses how AI systems create ripple effects across society, struggles to measure risk accurately, and ignores that powerful nations shape global AI rules. The authors suggest viewing AI as an active force that reshapes society itself, rather than just a tool to control, would lead to better regulation.
explain_business: Risk-based AI regulation, while providing clear compliance categories, may create false confidence and regulatory arbitrage opportunities. Organizations should anticipate that current frameworks will evolve as policymakers recognize measurement limitations and unintended consequences of deployment. Companies should prepare for more sophisticated, adaptive regulatory approaches that treat AI as a structural force, not merely a controllable tool. This suggests investing in broader stakeholder engagement and impact monitoring beyond checklist compliance.
explain_practitioner: The study examines risk-based AI regulation frameworks, particularly the EU AI Act, and identifies structural gaps. The analysis reveals that categorical risk assessment fails to capture feedback loops between AI deployment and social structures, measurement uncertainty undermines classification reliability, and geopolitical asymmetries influence regulatory design. The authors propose structuration theory as an analytical framework, positioning AI systems as active agents that co-constitute social structures, offering a more comprehensive lens for regulatory development that acknowledges AI's recursive influence on institutional and social arrangements.
